data.name: DayNight_Globe_Fact1
data.value: Sunlight reaches Earth in parallel rays, so at any moment exactly half of Earth is lit. The edge of the lit half is a great circle: the circle of illumination.

data.name: DayNight_Globe_Fact2
data.value: The circle always stands at right angles to the sunlight. Because Earth's axis is tilted, it passes through the poles only at the equinoxes; at the solstices it leans 23.4° from the axis and just touches the polar circles.

data.name: DayNight_Globe_Fact3
data.value: Inside the polar circle tilted towards the Sun, Earth's turn never carries you out of the lit half: the Sun does not set (polar day). Inside the other one it does not rise (polar night).

data.name: DayNight_Globe_Fact4
data.value: On the flat map the same circle looks like a wave, because the map stretches the regions near the poles sideways.

data.name: DayNight_Globe_Fact5
data.value: Seen from above the North Pole, Earth turns anticlockwise, from west to east. That is why the Sun rises in the east, and places further east see it first.

data.name: DayNight_Map_Fact1
data.value: The edge of the lit half is the terminator. West of the Sun it is the sunrise line, where the day is beginning; east of it the sunset line, where it is ending.

data.name: DayNight_Map_Fact2
data.value: Earth turns once in 24 hours, 15° an hour, so the lit half sweeps west 15° every hour: at the equator that is about 1,670 km an hour.

data.name: DayNight_Map_Fact3
data.value: Dark does not come at sunset. Civil twilight lasts until the Sun is 6° below the horizon, and the sky is fully dark only once it is 18° below. Near the polar circles, summer nights never get fully dark.

data.name: DayNight_Map_Fact4
data.value: The line's shape follows the seasons: straight from pole to pole at the equinoxes, a wave that touches the polar circles at the solstices, with polar day on one side and polar night on the other.

data.name: DayNight_Map_Fact5
data.value: Sunrise and sunset are counted from the top edge of the Sun, and the air bends its light up by about half a degree, so even at an equinox the day is a few minutes longer than 12 hours.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Fact1
data.value: Until the 19th century every town kept its own solar time. Railways and the telegraph needed one time: in 1884 the world agreed on Greenwich as 0°, and later on zones 15° (one hour) wide.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Fact2
data.value: Real zones follow borders. China spans about 60° of longitude, five ideal zones, yet all of it keeps Beijing time (UTC+8): in Kashgar the Sun is highest close to 15:00.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Fact3
data.value: Some zones are off by half or a quarter of an hour: India keeps UTC+5:30 and Nepal UTC+5:45.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Fact4
data.value: At any moment two dates are in use, and for two hours each day even three. A new date begins at midnight and spreads west; it ends at the international date line, which runs roughly along 180°.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Fact5
data.value: Kiritimati (UTC+14) and Honolulu (UTC−10) lie almost on the same meridian: their clocks show the same time, a whole day apart.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Fact6
data.value: Daylight saving puts clocks an hour ahead in summer, as in London, New York and Sydney. China does not use it.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Note
data.value: Ideal time zones 15° wide; real zones follow borders. Cities show the time on their real clocks, daylight saving included.

data.name: DayNight_TimeZones_Subtitle
data.value: Clocks follow the Sun: every 15° east, an hour later

data.name: Eclipse_Lunar_Fact3

data.name: Eclipse_Seasons_Fact1
data.value: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5.1° to the plane of Earth's orbit (the ecliptic); the picture exaggerates the tilt. The two planes cross along the line of nodes.

data.name: Eclipse_Seasons_Fact2
data.value: Most months the new moon passes a little above or below the Sun, and the full moon above or below Earth's shadow, so nothing happens.

data.name: Eclipse_Seasons_Fact3
data.value: Twice a year the line of nodes points at the Sun. These eclipse seasons last about 34 days, longer than a month (29.5 days), so each brings at least one solar eclipse: there are 2 to 5 a year.

data.name: Eclipse_Seasons_Fact4
data.value: The line of nodes slowly turns, once every 18.6 years, so the eclipse seasons come about 19 days earlier each year. The picture leaves this out.

data.name: Eclipse_Seasons_Subtitle
data.value: Why not every month? Because the Moon's orbit is tilted

data.name: Eclipse_Solar_Fact1
data.value: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon and about 400 times farther away, so the two look almost the same size in the sky: just enough for the Moon to cover the Sun.

data.name: Eclipse_Solar_Fact2
data.value: A solar eclipse can only happen at new moon. The Moon's umbra is small, so totality is seen only along a narrow path, usually 100–200 km wide; on either side people see a partial eclipse.

data.name: Eclipse_Solar_Fact3
data.value: Totality lasts a few minutes at most, never more than about 7½. At any one place a total eclipse comes round only once every few hundred years on average.

data.name: Eclipse_Solar_Fact4
data.value: Never look at the Sun directly, or through a camera, binoculars or a telescope, without a proper solar filter, not even when most of it is covered. Only during totality is it safe to look.

data.name: Eclipse_Solar_Subtitle
data.value: Solar eclipse: at new moon, the Moon's shadow falls on Earth

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_InSeason_Description
data.value: The line of nodes points (nearly) at the Sun. For about five weeks the new and full moons fall close to the ecliptic, so eclipses happen.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_LunarNone_Description

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_LunarPartial_Description
data.value: Part of the Moon is in Earth's umbra and looks as if a dark bite had been taken out of it.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_LunarPenumbral_Description
data.value: The Moon is in Earth's penumbra, where only part of the Sun is hidden. It dims a little, which is easy to miss with the naked eye.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_LunarTotal_Description
data.value: The whole Moon is in Earth's umbra. It does not go black: sunlight bent through Earth's atmosphere still reaches it, and as the blue is scattered away on the way, the Moon glows copper red.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_OutOfSeason_Description
data.value: The line of nodes points away from the Sun. At new and full moon the Moon passes above or below the Sun or Earth's shadow, so there is no eclipse.

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_SolarAnnular_Description

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_SolarNone_Description

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_SolarPartial_Description

data.name: Eclipse_Stage_SolarTotal_Description
data.value: You are in the Moon's umbra: the Sun is completely hidden. The sky turns dark, bright stars and planets appear, and the Sun's pearly corona shines around the black Moon.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact1
data.value: Kepler actually found this law first, in 1609, before he knew the orbit was an ellipse.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact2
data.value: Equal areas means the planet's angular momentum stays the same: at half the distance it goes twice as fast sideways. A spinning skater who pulls in their arms speeds up for the same reason.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact3
data.value: Earth is fastest in early January (30.3 km/s) and slowest in early July (29.3 km/s).

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact4
data.value: So the northern summer half of the year, from the March to the September equinox, is about 7 days longer than the winter half.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Fact5
data.value: Halley's comet races past the Sun at about 55 km/s, and crawls at under 1 km/s far out, where it spends most of its 75 years.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Note
data.value: Each coloured slice takes the same time. Near the Sun they are short and wide, far out long and thin, but all have the same area. Not to scale.

data.name: Kepler_Areas_Subtitle
data.value: Second law: the line from the Sun to the planet sweeps equal areas in equal times

data.value: Drag to move the planet along its orbit

data.name: Kepler_Earth_Note
data.value: From Earth's orbit, to within a day or two. Earth is closest to the Sun in the northern winter: the seasons come from the tilt of its axis, not from the distance.

data.name: Kepler_Ecc_Note
data.value: c is how far the Sun is from the centre, a half the long axis. The planets are all near 0: their orbits are almost circles, just with the Sun a little off centre. Moving the slider shapes the example orbit.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact1
data.value: Kepler found the ellipse in 1609 from Tycho Brahe's measurements of Mars: a circle missed them by 8 arcminutes, a quarter of the Moon's width, and he would not ignore it.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact2
data.value: Earth's orbit is nearly a circle (e = 0.017): its distance from the Sun only goes from 147.1 to 152.1 million km.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact3
data.value: The Sun sits at one focus; the other is just an empty point in space. The centre of the ellipse is empty too.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact4
data.value: Newton showed in 1687 why: a pull that weakens with the square of the distance gives ellipses, or for anything fast enough to escape, open curves that never come back.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Fact5
data.value: Halley's comet (e = 0.967) goes from inside Venus's orbit to beyond Neptune's. It was last near the Sun in 1986 and comes back in 2061.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Note
data.value: Like drawing with two pins and a loop of string: the two parts of the string always add up to the same length. Not to scale: the Sun and the planet are drawn far too big.

data.name: Kepler_Ellipse_Subtitle
data.value: First law: a planet goes round the Sun on an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus

data.name: Kepler_PeriodChart_Note
data.value: On logarithmic scales T² = a³ is a straight line, rising 3 for every 2 across. Every planet, the dwarf planets and Halley's comet sit on it: one rule for everything going round the Sun.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact1
data.value: Kepler published the third law in 1619, ten years after the first two, in his book Harmonices Mundi (The Harmony of the World).

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact2
data.value: Twice as far means 2.8 times as long a year: the path is twice as long and the planet goes 1.4 times slower.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact3
data.value: Neptune takes 165 years: discovered in 1846, it finished its first round since then only in 2011.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact4
data.value: Newton's version includes the mass in the middle, so a moon's orbit weighs its planet: that is how we know Jupiter's mass.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Fact5
data.value: It works for satellites too: 42,164 km from Earth's centre one round takes 23 h 56 min, just as long as Earth takes to turn, so a geostationary satellite stays over one spot.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Note
data.value: Distances to scale: the planets at their real places today, seen from above the Sun's north pole. The view zooms out to keep your planet in sight; the planets are drawn far too big.

data.name: Kepler_Periods_Subtitle
data.value: Third law: the square of a planet's year goes with the cube of its distance

data.name: Kepler_Speed_Note
data.value: Where the distance is smallest the speed is greatest, and the other way round: distance times sideways speed stays the same all the way.

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Aphelion_Description
data.value: Farthest from the Sun and slowest. It does not stop: still moving sideways, it begins to fall back towards the Sun.

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Approaching_Description

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Circle

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Circle_Description

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Perihelion_Description

data.name: Kepler_Stage_Receding_Description

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_FirstQuarter_Description
data.value: A quarter of the way round: we see half of the lit half. It is due south at sunset and sets around midnight.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_Full_Description
data.value: Earth is between the Sun and the Moon: the whole lit half faces us. It rises at sunset and is up all night.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_LastQuarter_Description
data.value: Three quarters of the way round: half lit again, the other half. It rises around midnight and is due south at sunrise.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_New_Description
data.value: The Moon is between Earth and the Sun: its lit half faces away from us. It crosses the sky with the Sun, lost in its glare.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_WaningCrescent_Description
data.value: Only a sliver of the lit half still faces us. Look low in the east just before sunrise.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_WaningGibbous_Description

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_WaxingCrescent_Description

data.name: MoonPhases_Phase_WaxingGibbous_Description
data.value: More than half the disc is lit and growing. It rises in the afternoon and is up most of the evening.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact1
data.value: The Moon makes no light of its own. Like Earth, it is always half lit by the Sun; the phase is how much of that lit half faces us.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact2
data.value: The phases are not Earth's shadow: at a crescent, Earth's shadow points far away from the Moon. Earth's shadow only falls on the Moon in a lunar eclipse.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact3
data.value: Eclipses can only happen at new moon (solar) and full moon (lunar), yet most months there is none: the Moon's orbit is tilted 5°, so it usually passes above or below.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact4
data.value: The Moon turns once on its axis each time it goes round Earth, so it always shows us the same face. The far side is not dark: it is fully lit at new moon.

data.name: MoonPhases_Phases_Fact5
data.value: Waxing (growing) phases are lit on the right, waning ones on the left, as seen from the northern hemisphere; from the southern hemisphere it is the other way round.

data.name: Narr_Common_MoveOn
data.value: Let's keep going. You can try it again later.

data.name: Narr_Common_Reveal
data.value: Time's up! Here's the right answer.

data.name: Narr_Common_Wrong
data.value: Not quite. Let's look at the answer.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_01
data.value: Now let's look at a globe. Sunlight comes in from the left, and it can only ever light up half of Earth at a time.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_02
data.value: The edge between the lit half and the dark half is a great circle. As Earth spins once a day, every place passes through it twice, once at sunrise and once at sunset.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_03
data.value: Earth's axis is tilted. So, except at the equinoxes, this circle doesn't pass through the poles. It's turned away from the axis by an angle.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_04
data.value: Let's jump to June. Now that angle is at its largest, about twenty-three and a half degrees, the same as the tilt of the axis.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_05
data.value: Look near the North Pole. However Earth turns, it stays in the lit half all day long. That's polar day, the midnight sun. Near the South Pole it stays dark all day: polar night.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_06
data.value: Quick question. In December, where is there polar day?

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Globe_07
data.value: It's near the South Pole. In December the southern half leans towards the Sun, so the South Pole has polar day, and the North Pole has its long polar night. Drag the globe to look at it from another angle.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_01
data.value: This is a map of the whole world. The bright part is in daylight and the dark part is in night. The curved gold line between them is where day meets night.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_02
data.value: Right here the Sun is straight overhead. Earth spins from west to east, so the Sun seems to slide west, fifteen degrees every hour, all the way round in a day.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_03
data.value: On this half of the line, the Sun is rising right now. It's called the sunrise line. On the other half, the sunset line, the Sun is going down.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_04
data.value: Everywhere on the gold vertical line it's noon, and everywhere on the blue one it's midnight. Both lines slide west along with the Sun.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_05
data.value: Think about it. If you lived further east, would you see sunrise earlier or later?

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_06
data.value: The answer is earlier: the sunrise line reaches the east first. Now let's run through a whole year, stopping at the same moment each day. Watch the line change shape. Around June the north has the long days, around December the south does, and only at the equinoxes does the line run straight from pole to pole.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_07
data.value: Now you try. Click a city on the map, and the left page shows what time it is there and how high the Sun is.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Map_08
data.value: Wherever you are, sunrise, noon and sunset all come from the same thing: Earth turning you towards the Sun and away again.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Angle
data.value: The angle between the axis and the edge of the lit half. It's the same as how far north or south of the equator the Sun is overhead: zero at the equinoxes, about twenty-three and a half degrees at the solstices.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Axis
data.value: Earth's axis, through the North and South Poles. It's tilted about twenty-three and a half degrees, which is why day length changes through the year.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_DateLine
data.value: The international date line, mostly along one hundred and eighty degrees. Going east across it, you set your calendar back a day; going west, forward a day.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Equator
data.value: The equator. On it, day and night are about twelve hours each, all year round.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Midnight
data.value: Everywhere under this line it's midnight by the Sun, halfway between sunset and sunrise.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_NewDay
data.value: This is where it's midnight. East of it, the date has already changed. The new day spreads west by one zone every hour.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Noon
data.value: Everywhere under this line it's noon by the Sun: the Sun is at its highest point of the day.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_PolarCircle
data.value: The polar circles, about sixty-six and a half degrees north and south. Inside them there's at least one day a year without sunset, and one without sunrise.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_PolarDay
data.value: Polar day. Here the whole circle of latitude stays in the lit half as Earth turns, so the Sun never sets.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_PolarNight
data.value: Polar night. Here the whole circle of latitude stays in the dark half, so the Sun never rises.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Sun
data.value: This is where the Sun is straight overhead. It moves west fifteen degrees every hour, and over the year it wanders between the two tropics.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Sunlight
data.value: Sunlight from far away arrives as parallel rays, so it lights exactly half of Earth at any moment.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_SunriseLine
data.value: The sunrise line. Everywhere along it, the Sun is just coming up. It sweeps west across the world as Earth turns.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_SunsetLine
data.value: The sunset line. Everywhere along it, the Sun is just going down, and evening is beginning.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Tropics
data.value: The tropics, about twenty-three and a half degrees north and south. They're as far from the equator as the Sun is ever overhead.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Utc
data.value: UTC is world time, kept by atomic clocks and almost exactly the time at Greenwich in London. Every time zone is a whole number of hours ahead of it or behind it, with a few exceptions.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Obj_Zone
data.value: This is the time zone of the place you've picked. Each zone is about fifteen degrees of longitude, one hour of the Sun's journey.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Zones_01
data.value: If every town set its clocks by its own Sun, even neighbouring towns would be a few minutes apart. So the world is divided by longitude into twenty-four time zones, each about fifteen degrees wide.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Zones_02
data.value: The numbers along the top show how many hours each zone is ahead of or behind world time, called UTC. Along the bottom is the time on clocks there right now.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Zones_03
data.value: Look at this blue line. It's where midnight is right now. East of it, a new day has already begun, and the new date spreads west by one time zone every hour.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Zones_04
data.value: Think about it. Where does each new date begin first?

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Zones_05
data.value: A new date begins first just west of the international date line, out in the middle of the Pacific. Cross the line going east and you go back a day. Cross it going west and you jump forward a day.

data.name: Narr_DayNight_Zones_06
data.value: Time zones follow borders, not just longitude. China spans about five zones but uses Beijing time everywhere, so in the far west the Sun rises very late by the clock.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_01
data.value: Now it's Earth's turn to cast a shadow. Like the Moon's, it points straight away from the Sun, out into space.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_02
data.value: When the Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, it's full moon. That's the only time it can pass through Earth's shadow.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_03
data.value: Earth's umbra is much wider than the Moon, so the whole Moon fits inside it. That's why a total lunar eclipse can last for more than an hour.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_04
data.value: Now the Moon is deep in Earth's umbra. Think about it: what colour does it turn?

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_05
data.value: Copper red. Earth's air bends a little sunlight into the shadow, and on the way the blue light is scattered away, just like at sunset. In a way, the Moon is lit by all the sunrises and sunsets on Earth at once.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_06
data.value: And unlike a solar eclipse, everyone on the night side of Earth can see a lunar eclipse, all at the same time.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_07
data.value: Now you try. On the left page, choose a different path for the Moon through Earth's shadow, and watch how the eclipse changes.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Lunar_08
data.value: If the Moon only passes through the penumbra, it just dims a little. It's so faint that most people never notice.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Antumbra
data.value: The antumbra, beyond the tip of the umbra. From here, the Moon looks a little smaller than the Sun, so you see a ring of sunlight around it. That's an annular eclipse.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth. The side facing the Sun is in daytime. Its shadow points away from the Sun, and at full moon the Moon can pass through it.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Ecliptic
data.value: The plane of Earth's orbit, called the plane of the ecliptic. Seen from Earth, the Sun always moves along it.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_FullMoon
data.value: Full moon. Earth is between the Sun and the Moon, and we see the Moon's whole lit side. Only now can a lunar eclipse happen.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Moon
data.value: The Moon. At new moon its shadow can fall on Earth, and at full moon it can move into Earth's shadow. In the side views you can drag it around its orbit.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_MoonOrbit
data.value: The Moon's orbit, tilted by about five degrees, drawn steeper here. The solid half is above the plane of Earth's orbit, and the dashed half is below.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_NewMoon
data.value: New moon. The Moon is between the Sun and Earth, and its lit side faces away from us. Only now can a solar eclipse happen.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_NodeLine
data.value: The line of nodes, joining the two points where the Moon crosses the plane of Earth's orbit. When it points at the Sun, it's eclipse season.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Observer
data.value: This is you, on Earth's day side, where it's around noon. On the left page, you can move north or south and see how the eclipse looks from there.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Penumbra
data.value: The penumbra, the lighter shadow around the umbra. From here, only part of the Sun is hidden.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Season
data.value: An eclipse season. While Earth is on this stretch of its orbit, the line of nodes points close to the Sun, and eclipses can happen.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun. It's about four hundred times wider than the Moon, and about four hundred times farther away. That's why the two look almost the same size in our sky.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Obj_Umbra
data.value: The umbra, the darkest part of a shadow. From inside it, the Sun is completely hidden.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_01
data.value: If there's a new moon every month, why isn't there a solar eclipse every month? Here's Earth going round the Sun over a year, with the Moon going round Earth.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_02
data.value: Look at the Moon's orbit. It's tilted, really by about five degrees, drawn steeper here so you can see it. The solid blue half is above the plane of Earth's orbit, and the dashed orange half is below it.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_03
data.value: The Moon crosses the plane of Earth's orbit at two points, called nodes. The line joining them is the line of nodes.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_04
data.value: Think about it. In most months, what happens at new moon?

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_05
data.value: Most of the time, the Moon passes just above or below the Sun, so its shadow misses Earth. For an eclipse, the new or full moon has to fall close to a node.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_06
data.value: That only happens when the line of nodes points towards the Sun: twice a year, for about five weeks each time. These are the eclipse seasons.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_07
data.value: Every eclipse season brings at least one solar eclipse somewhere on Earth, and often a lunar eclipse too. That's why there are between four and seven eclipses every year.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag across the picture to move through the year, and find the next eclipse season.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Seasons_09
data.value: The line of nodes slowly turns, so the eclipse seasons come about nineteen days earlier each year.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_01
data.value: This is a view from far above. The Sun is on the left, Earth on the right, and the Moon goes round Earth. The sizes and distances aren't to scale, or the Sun would be far off the screen.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_02
data.value: The Moon goes round Earth about once a month. When it passes between the Sun and Earth, we call it new moon.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_03
data.value: Like everything in sunlight, the Moon casts a shadow. The darkest part is called the umbra. Inside it, the Sun is completely hidden.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_04
data.value: Around it is a lighter shadow, the penumbra. From there, the Moon covers only part of the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_05
data.value: Now the Moon's shadow falls on Earth. Think about it: if you stood right inside the umbra, what would you see?

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_06
data.value: A total solar eclipse. The sky goes dark, bright stars come out, and the Sun's pearly corona glows around the black Moon. The umbra only covers a narrow strip of Earth, so most people see a partial eclipse instead.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_07
data.value: The Moon's distance from Earth changes a little. When it's farther away, its umbra is too short to reach Earth. Then we see an annular eclipse: a ring of fire around the Moon.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag the Moon around its orbit, and watch its shadow sweep across Earth.

data.name: Narr_Eclipse_Solar_09
data.value: So a solar eclipse can only happen at new moon. At full moon, it's the Moon's turn to move into Earth's shadow. That's a lunar eclipse.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_01
data.value: Kepler's second law is about speed. Imagine a line from the Sun to the planet. As the planet moves, this line sweeps across the orbit, a bit like a windscreen wiper.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_02
data.value: The orbit is cut into twelve coloured slices. The planet takes exactly the same time to cross each one: one twelfth of its year.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_03
data.value: Compare these two slices. Near the Sun, the slice is short and wide. Far away, it's long and thin. But their areas are exactly the same.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_04
data.value: So in the same amount of time, the planet covers much more of its orbit when it's near the Sun. This orange arrow shows its speed. Watch it grow and shrink.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_05
data.value: Think about it. Where does the planet move fastest?

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_06
data.value: Closest to the Sun. That point is called perihelion. The farthest point is aphelion, where the planet is slowest. Earth does this too: in early January it moves about one kilometre per second faster than in early July.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_07
data.value: Now you try. Drag the planet around its orbit with the mouse, and watch how its speed changes.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Areas_08
data.value: Halley's comet shows this most of all. It rushes past the Sun in a few months, then crawls through the far end of its orbit for decades. That's Kepler's second law: equal areas in equal times.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_01
data.value: This loop is an orbit, the path a planet takes around the Sun. Look closely: it isn't a circle. It's an ellipse, a circle that's been stretched.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_02
data.value: And the Sun isn't in the middle. It sits off to one side, at a special point called a focus.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_03
data.value: An ellipse has two foci. The other one is over here, and it's completely empty. Nothing at all is there.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_04
data.value: Now picture a loop of string pinned at both foci, with a pencil pulling it tight. The gold part runs from the Sun to the planet, and the blue part from the planet to the empty focus.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_05
data.value: Here the planet is at its closest to the Sun, so the gold part is short. Think about it: what about the blue part?

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_06
data.value: It's longer. Wherever the planet goes, the two parts always add up to the same length: the long axis of the ellipse. That's how gardeners mark out an oval flower bed, with two pegs and a loop of rope.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_07
data.value: Now you try. Move the orbit shape slider on the left page. Make the orbit rounder, or more stretched, and watch the empty focus move.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Ellipse_08
data.value: This is Earth's real orbit. It's so close to a circle that you can hardly tell the difference. That's Kepler's first law: every planet moves on an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Aphelion
data.value: Aphelion, the point farthest from the Sun. Here the planet moves slowest. Earth passes it in early July.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Center
data.value: The centre of the ellipse. Neither focus is here: the Sun sits off to one side.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Circle
data.value: A circle of the same size, to compare. The more the orbit is stretched, the further it strays from this circle.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth, our home. One trip round the Sun is one year, about three hundred and sixty-five days.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_EqualAreas
data.value: Each coloured slice takes the same time and has the same area. That's Kepler's second law.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_FocalDistance
data.value: This is how far the Sun sits from the centre. Divide it by half the long axis and you get the eccentricity: zero for a circle, and close to one for a very stretched orbit.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Jupiter
data.value: Jupiter, about five times as far from the Sun as Earth. It takes almost twelve years to go round once.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_MajorAxis
data.value: The long axis of the ellipse, from one end to the other. Half of it is the planet's average distance from the Sun, and that sets how long its year is.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Mars
data.value: Mars, about one and a half times as far from the Sun as Earth. Its year is almost two of ours.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Mercury
data.value: Mercury, the closest planet to the Sun. It goes round in just eighty-eight days, faster than any other planet.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_OtherFocus
data.value: The other focus. Nothing is here at all, no star and no planet. It's just a point that belongs to the shape of the ellipse.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Perihelion
data.value: Perihelion, the point of the orbit closest to the Sun. Here the planet moves fastest. Earth passes it in early January.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Planet
data.value: The body going round the Sun. You can drag it along its orbit with the mouse.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Saturn
data.value: Saturn, nearly ten times as far from the Sun as Earth. It goes round once in about twenty-nine and a half years.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Scale
data.value: The scale bar. One astronomical unit is the distance from Earth to the Sun, about a hundred and fifty million kilometres.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_String
data.value: The string. One part runs from the Sun to the planet, the other from the planet to the empty focus. As one grows, the other shrinks, but together they always make the same length.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun. Its gravity keeps every planet on its orbit. Notice that it isn't at the centre of an orbit, but at one of its two foci.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Velocity
data.value: The planet's speed right now, in kilometres per second. The arrow points the way it's going.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_Venus
data.value: Venus, the second planet. Its year is about two hundred and twenty-five days, and its orbit is almost a perfect circle.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Obj_You
data.value: Your planet. Drag it nearer to the Sun or farther away, and its year changes to follow Kepler's third law.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_01
data.value: Now let's compare planets. Here are the planets out to Saturn, seen from above, at their real places today. Earth goes round once in one year.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_02
data.value: Mercury, closest to the Sun, needs only eighty-eight days. The farther out, the longer the year: Mars takes almost two years, and Jupiter almost twelve.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_03
data.value: This green dot is a planet of your own. It started out in line with Earth, but it's farther from the Sun, so it slowly falls behind.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_04
data.value: Think about it. If your planet were four times as far from the Sun as Earth, how long would its year be?

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_05
data.value: Eight years. Kepler found that the year, squared, equals the distance, cubed. Four cubed is sixty-four, and eight squared is sixty-four too. Planets farther out have a longer way to go, and they also move more slowly.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_06
data.value: Now you try. Drag your planet nearer to the Sun or farther away, and see how long its year becomes.

data.name: Narr_Kepler_Periods_07
data.value: This rule works for every planet. Later, Isaac Newton showed where it comes from: the Sun's gravity gets weaker the farther away you are. The table on the left page checks it for each planet.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Month_01
data.value: From one new moon to the next takes twenty-nine and a half days. But the Moon only needs about twenty-seven days to go once around Earth. So where do the extra two days come from?

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Month_02
data.value: Let's measure against a very distant star. This dashed white line always points at that same star.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Month_03
data.value: After twenty-seven point three days, the Moon is back in line with that star. It has gone once around Earth. But look: it isn't between Earth and the Sun yet, so it isn't a new moon.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Month_04
data.value: Think about it. Why isn't it there yet?

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Month_05
data.value: During the month, Earth has carried the Moon a good way around the Sun, so the direction of the Sun has turned by this angle. The Moon needs about two more days to catch up.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Month_06
data.value: At twenty-nine and a half days, the Moon is between Earth and the Sun again, and the new moon is back. So a full round of phases takes about two days longer than one trip around Earth.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Earth
data.value: This is Earth, seen from far above the North Pole. Its day side faces the Sun on the left. From here we watch the Moon go round.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_EarthOrbit
data.value: This is Earth, moving along its orbit around the Sun. As it moves, the direction of the Sun seen from Earth slowly turns.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_FirstQuarter
data.value: First quarter. Half of the face we see is lit. The Moon has gone a quarter of the way round, and it's high in the sky at sunset.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Full
data.value: Full moon. The Moon is on the far side of Earth from the Sun, and its whole lit half faces us. It rises at sunset and shines all night.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_LastQuarter
data.value: Last quarter. Half lit again, but the other half this time. It rises around midnight and is still up in the morning sky.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Moon
data.value: This is the Moon. The gold arc marks its lit half, and the dashed blue arc marks the half facing Earth. The phase is simply how much of the lit half we can see.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_MoonOrbit
data.value: This is the Moon going round Earth. It always keeps the same face towards us, so we never see its far side from Earth.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Moonrise
data.value: These are the times the Moon rises and sets today. On average it rises about fifty minutes later each day, because it moves round Earth in the same direction Earth spins.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_New
data.value: New moon. The Moon is between Earth and the Sun, with its dark side towards us, so we can't see it.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Sidereal
data.value: After twenty-seven point three days the Moon has gone once around Earth, measured against the stars. This is called a sidereal month.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_SkyMoon
data.value: This is the Moon in your sky. Its bright side always points back towards the Sun, even when the Sun is below the horizon.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_SkySun
data.value: This is the Sun. Each day the Moon lags behind it a little more, which is why the Moon rises later every day.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Star
data.value: This is a very distant star. It's so far away that it lies in the same direction from anywhere on Earth's orbit, which makes it a perfect fixed marker.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Start
data.value: This is where the month starts: a new moon, with the Moon between Earth and the Sun.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Sun
data.value: This is the Sun. Earth goes round it once a year, so in one month Earth covers about a twelfth of its orbit.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Sunlight
data.value: Sunlight comes from the left. The Sun is so far away that its rays arrive almost parallel, lighting half of Earth and half of the Moon at all times.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_Synodic
data.value: After twenty-nine point five days the Moon is back between Earth and the Sun: new moon again. This is called a synodic month, the month of the phases.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_WaningCrescent
data.value: Waning crescent. A thin curve seen in the east before sunrise, getting thinner until the next new moon.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_WaningGibbous
data.value: Waning gibbous. Just after full, the bright part starts to shrink, and the Moon rises later each evening.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_WaxingCrescent
data.value: Waxing crescent. A thin bright curve appears in the west just after sunset, and it grows a little every night.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Obj_WaxingGibbous
data.value: Waxing gibbous. More than half is lit, and it's still growing towards full.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_01
data.value: Why does the Moon change shape through the month? It doesn't make any light of its own. What we see is the part lit up by the Sun.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_02
data.value: Sunlight comes in from the left. Wherever the Moon is, the half facing the Sun is always lit, and the other half is dark.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_03
data.value: Look at the two arcs beside the Moon. The gold one marks the lit half. The dashed blue one marks the half facing Earth. Where they overlap is the bright part we can see.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_04
data.value: When the Moon passes between Earth and the Sun, its lit half faces completely away from us. We can hardly see it at all. That's the new moon.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_05
data.value: Think about it. When the Moon moves round to the far side of Earth, away from the Sun, what will we see?

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_06
data.value: It's a full moon. Now the lit half faces Earth completely, so the whole round face shines.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_07
data.value: Now you try. Drag the Moon round until exactly half of it looks lit, a first quarter. Or just click its picture in the outer ring.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_08
data.value: The outer ring shows how the Moon looks from Earth. From new to full, the bright part grows day by day. From full back to new, it shrinks again. The whole round takes about twenty-nine and a half days.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Phases_09
data.value: So the phases aren't made by Earth's shadow. We're simply seeing the Moon's lit half from different angles. Click the little pictures in the outer ring to hear about each phase.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_01
data.value: Now we're standing on the ground, looking across the sky towards the equator. Every day the Sun rises in the east, crosses the sky along this dashed line, and sets in the west.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_02
data.value: The Moon travels the same road, just later than the Sun. This is a first quarter moon. It rises around midday, and it's high in the sky when the Sun sets.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_03
data.value: A full moon sits opposite the Sun. As the Sun goes down in the west, the full moon comes up in the east. It stays up all night and sets around dawn.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_04
data.value: Quick question. At new moon, when is the Moon up in the sky?

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_05
data.value: A new moon is in almost the same direction as the Sun, so it crosses the sky with the Sun in the daytime. Its dark side faces us, and it's lost in the Sun's glare, so we don't notice it at all.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_06
data.value: Now let's look at the same time every evening. Each day the Moon has moved a little further east and grown a little fatter. It rises about fifty minutes later each day.

data.name: Narr_MoonPhases_Sky_07
data.value: So the Moon's shape tells you roughly when it rises and sets. Drag across the picture to change the time and go looking for the Moon.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_01
data.value: Now let's fly far above the Sun and look down. Here are the orbits of Earth and Mars, drawn to scale. They both go round the same way.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_02
data.value: Earth is on the inside lane. It has a shorter way to go, and it moves faster, about thirty kilometres every second.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_03
data.value: This line is our line of sight: from Earth, through Mars, on towards the distant stars. Its direction is where we see Mars in the sky.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_04
data.value: The numbers mark the line of sight at different moments. In the circle in the corner, they're all drawn from one point, because the stars are so far away that only the direction counts. One, then two: the line turns forward, so Mars drifts east.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_05
data.value: Now Earth catches up with Mars, and overtakes it on the inside. At three, the line stops turning. At four and five, it has swung backwards. That's the retrograde loop.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_06
data.value: So, why does Mars seem to go backwards?

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_07
data.value: Once Earth is past, the line swings forward again. Mars never really reverses. It's like overtaking a slower car on the motorway: for a moment, it seems to slide backwards against the hills far away.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_08
data.value: For Mercury and Venus, it's the other way round. They're on the inside lane, so they overtake us, and they go backwards as they pass between Earth and the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Above_09
data.value: Your turn. Drag Earth round its orbit and watch the line of sight, or try another planet.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_01
data.value: For almost two thousand years, people put Earth at the centre of everything. Let's do the same. Hold Earth still, and see where Mars goes.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_02
data.value: Mars draws loop after loop, roughly one every two years. And every loop comes when Mars is closest to us.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_03
data.value: The ancient astronomer Ptolemy explained this with circles. Mars rides on a small circle, the epicycle, and the centre of that circle goes round a big one, the deferent.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_04
data.value: Here's the surprise. The epicycle is just Earth's own orbit, seen from Earth. Its arm always points the same way as the Sun, and it turns once a year.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_05
data.value: What do you think happens if we hold the Sun still instead?

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_06
data.value: Copernicus put the Sun in the middle. Watch the loops untangle into a plain, almost circular orbit. The same motion, but a much simpler picture.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_07
data.value: Back to Earth at the centre, this time with Venus. Over eight years, Venus loops five times and draws a five-petalled flower, then starts again almost exactly where it began.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Epicycle_08
data.value: Your turn. Switch between Earth and the Sun at the centre, or choose another planet and watch its pattern grow.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Conjunction
data.value: Inferior conjunction: the planet passes between Earth and the Sun. It's lost in the Sun's glare, at its closest to us, and going backwards fastest.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Deferent
data.value: The deferent: Ptolemy's big circle round Earth. The centre of the epicycle rides round it.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth, our moving viewpoint. Because we watch from a planet that is itself going round the Sun, the other planets seem to loop.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_EarthOrbit
data.value: Earth's orbit: one lap a year, at about thirty kilometres every second.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_East
data.value: East among the stars. This is the way the planets usually drift, night after night, and the way the Sun and the Moon move against the stars too.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Ecliptic
data.value: The ecliptic: the Sun's path round the sky in a year. The planets' orbits lie almost in the same plane as Earth's, so they always wander close to it.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Epicycle
data.value: The epicycle: the small circle the planet rides on. For Mars, Jupiter and Saturn it is really Earth's own orbit in disguise. For Mercury and Venus it is the planet's own orbit round the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Fan
data.value: The lines of sight, all drawn from one point. The stars are so far away that only a line's direction matters, so here you can see the line turn forward, then back, then forward again.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Frame
data.value: What is held still in the middle. With Earth still, the planets loop. With the Sun still, they go round in plain orbits. Either way, it's the very same motion.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Jupiter
data.value: Jupiter, the giant. It moves so slowly that Earth laps it about every thirteen months, and each time it goes backwards for about four months.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Loop
data.value: A retrograde loop, seen from Earth. Each one comes when Earth and the planet are at their closest.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Marks
data.value: The line of sight at seven moments: before the loop, halfway to the first stop, at the first stop, in the middle, at the second stop, halfway on, and after.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Mars
data.value: Mars, the red planet, one step out from Earth. Earth overtakes it about every twenty-six months, and then it goes backwards for about ten weeks.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Mercury
data.value: Mercury, the planet nearest the Sun. It goes round in eighty-eight days and overtakes us three or four times a year, so it goes backwards more often than any other planet, for about three weeks each time.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Opposition
data.value: Opposition: the planet is opposite the Sun in our sky, with Earth right between them. It's up all night, near its closest and brightest, and going backwards fastest.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_PlanetOrbit
data.value: The planet's orbit, drawn to scale. The farther a planet is from the Sun, the slower it goes, and the longer its year.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Retro
data.value: The retrograde stretch. For these weeks the planet moves west against the stars, the opposite of its usual way.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Saturn
data.value: Saturn, the ringed planet. It's so slow that Earth passes it almost every year, and it spends about four and a half months going backwards.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Scale
data.value: A ruler for the sky. Ten degrees is about the width of your fist, held out at arm's length.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_SightLine
data.value: Our line of sight: from Earth, through the planet, on towards the far stars. Its direction is where we see the planet in the sky.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Speed
data.value: How fast each one moves along its orbit. The inner planet is always the faster one, so it's always the one that overtakes.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Stars
data.value: The background stars. Here they're drawn just outside the orbits, but really they're far, far away. Even the nearest one is more than a quarter of a million times farther than the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_StationDirect
data.value: The second station. The backward motion slows to a stop, and then the planet heads east again.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_StationRetro
data.value: The first station. The planet's eastward drift slows down to nothing, and it seems to stand still for a few days before it starts going backwards.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun. Every planet goes round it the same way. In our sky it moves steadily east along the ecliptic, and it never goes backwards.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Venus
data.value: Venus, the brightest planet. It goes backwards about every nineteen months, for some six weeks, as it passes between Earth and the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Obj_Zodiac
data.value: The zodiac constellations, the star patterns along the ecliptic. The Sun, the Moon and the planets all pass through them.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_01
data.value: This is a strip of the night sky along the zodiac, the band of stars the planets wander through. The bright dot is Mars. Let's watch it for a few months. Night after night, it creeps along among the stars.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_02
data.value: Most of the time, Mars drifts eastward, the way the gold arrow points. All the planets do, because they all go round the Sun in the same direction as Earth.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_03
data.value: But now, look. Mars slows down, and stops. For a few days it hardly moves against the stars at all. This is called a station.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_04
data.value: What do you think Mars does next?

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_05
data.value: It turns round and goes backwards, westward, for about ten weeks. Astronomers call this retrograde motion. The orange stretch is the backward part.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_06
data.value: Right in the middle of the backward stretch, Mars is opposite the Sun in our sky. It rises at sunset, shines all night, and is at its closest and brightest.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_07
data.value: Then it slows down, stops a second time, and turns east again, as if nothing had happened.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_08
data.value: Here's the whole path. Sometimes it's a loop, sometimes a zigzag, depending on how the planet's orbit is tilted against ours. And it always stays close to the ecliptic, the Sun's yearly path.

data.name: Narr_Retro_Sky_09
data.value: Your turn. Pick another planet and watch its loop, or drag across the sky to move through the days.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Distance_01
data.value: Lots of people think summer is warm because Earth is closer to the Sun. And Earth's path really isn't a perfect circle. It's a very slightly squashed oval.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Distance_02
data.value: So here's one for you to guess. In which month is Earth closest to the Sun?

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Distance_03
data.value: The answer is early January. That's when Earth is closest to the Sun, at a point called perihelion. Yet January is the coldest time of year in the north!

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Distance_04
data.value: And in early July, Earth is at its farthest, a point called aphelion. But that's the middle of summer in the north.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Distance_05
data.value: Over the year the distance changes by only about three percent, which hardly affects the temperature. So the seasons aren't really about distance. The real reason is the tilt of Earth's axis.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Aphelion
data.value: This is aphelion. Every year in early July, Earth is farthest from the Sun, about a hundred and fifty-two million kilometres away.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Axis
data.value: This line is Earth's axis, and it always points at the North Star. Because its direction never changes, the north and south take turns leaning towards the Sun as Earth goes around.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_December
data.value: This is the December solstice. The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Capricorn, so the north has its shortest day, and the south its longest.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Earth
data.value: This is Earth. It spins on its axis while it travels around the Sun. One spin is a day, and one trip around is a year. The gold line on it is your latitude.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Equinox
data.value: This is an equinox. On this day the axis leans neither towards the Sun nor away from it, so day and night are about the same length all over the world.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_June
data.value: This is the June solstice. The Sun is overhead at the Tropic of Cancer, so the north has its longest day, and the south its shortest.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Noon
data.value: This is where the Sun is at noon, its highest point of the day. The number beside it is how high it stands above the horizon.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Perihelion
data.value: This is perihelion. Every year in early January, Earth comes closest to the Sun, about a hundred and forty-seven million kilometres away.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Shadow
data.value: This is an upright post and its shadow. In a day, the shadow is shortest at noon. Over a year, noon shadows are shortest in summer and longest in winter.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_SkySun
data.value: This is where the Sun is right now. The higher it is above the horizon, the more directly its light hits the ground, and the more warmth the ground gets.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Sun
data.value: This is the Sun, the source of the energy behind the seasons. The Sun and Earth are drawn far bigger than they really are, or you couldn't see them.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Obj_Sunrise
data.value: This is where the Sun rises and sets. Only around the equinoxes does it rise due east and set due west. On other days it rises and sets further north or south.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_01
data.value: This time we're standing on the ground. The little post in the middle marks where you are, and the dome over it is your sky.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_02
data.value: Watch the Sun. It rises in the east, slowly arcs across the sky, and sets in the west. This gold curve is the path it takes today.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_03
data.value: The highest point of the curve is noon. The higher the Sun climbs, the more concentrated its light is, and the more it warms the ground.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_04
data.value: Now look at the post's shadow. When the Sun is high, the shadow is short. When it's low, the shadow is long. Long ago, people tracked the seasons by measuring shadows just like this.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_05
data.value: Now let's run time through a whole year instead. Look at the two dashed curves. In summer the Sun's path is high and long. In winter it's low and short.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_06
data.value: Think about it. Why is summer warmer than winter?

data.name: Narr_Seasons_SunPath_07
data.value: There are two reasons, working together. The Sun climbs higher, so its light is more concentrated, and the days are longer, so the ground warms for more hours. Drag left and right across the picture to move through the day yourself.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_01
data.value: Have you ever wondered why summer is warm and winter is cold? A lot of people guess it's because Earth gets closer to the Sun in summer. Let's find out together.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_02
data.value: In the middle is the Sun. Earth travels around it along this dashed path, and one trip around takes a whole year.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_03
data.value: Now look at the white line through Earth. It's called the axis, and Earth spins around it. Notice that it isn't upright. It leans over by about twenty-three and a half degrees.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_04
data.value: Here's the clever part. Wherever Earth is on its path, the axis always points the same way, towards the North Star. Keep your eye on it for a moment. It always leans to the upper right.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_05
data.value: Let's stop in June. Right now the northern half of Earth leans towards the Sun. The sunlight comes in more steeply, and the days are longer, so it's summer in the north.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_06
data.value: Now it's your turn. Drag Earth round to December, or just click on December, and see what happens to the north.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_07
data.value: In December the axis still points the same way, but now the north leans away from the Sun. The light arrives at a low slant, the days are short, and the north has winter. The south is the other way round. It's having summer.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_08
data.value: Quick question. What would happen if Earth's axis didn't lean at all?

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_09
data.value: Let's set the tilt to zero and see. Now every day of the year is much the same. The Sun is always overhead at the equator, day and night are equal, and the seasons disappear.

data.name: Narr_Seasons_Tilt_10
data.value: So the secret of the seasons isn't distance. It's the tilt of the axis. Try the sliders on the left page with a different tilt or latitude, and watch how the day length and the noon Sun on the card change.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Ariel
data.value: Ariel, one of the brightest moons of Uranus, crossed by long valleys.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Callisto
data.value: Callisto, one of the most heavily cratered worlds we know. Its surface has hardly changed for billions of years.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Deimos
data.value: Deimos, Mars's smaller moon, only about twelve kilometres across. Both of Mars's moons may be captured asteroids.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Dione
data.value: Dione, an icy moon of Saturn, its surface streaked with bright cliffs of ice.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Earth
data.value: Earth, our home, and the only place we know of with life. Most of its surface is covered by oceans of liquid water.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Enceladus
data.value: Enceladus, a small, bright moon of Saturn. Jets of water shoot out from cracks near its south pole, from an ocean hidden under the ice.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Europa
data.value: Europa, covered in a shell of ice. Underneath there's probably a deep ocean of salty water, one of the best places to look for life.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Ganymede
data.value: Ganymede, the biggest moon in the solar system, even bigger than the planet Mercury.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Iapetus
data.value: Iapetus, a two-faced moon: one side is as dark as coal, and the other as bright as snow.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Io
data.value: Io, the most volcanic place in the solar system. Jupiter's pull squeezes it so hard that hundreds of volcanoes keep erupting.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Jupiter
data.value: Jupiter, the biggest planet, a giant ball of gas. Its Great Red Spot is a storm bigger than Earth that has been raging for centuries.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Mars
data.value: Mars, the red planet. Rusty dust gives it its colour, and it has the tallest volcano in the solar system, Olympus Mons.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Mercury
data.value: Mercury, the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun. It has almost no air, so its days are hot enough to melt lead, and its nights are freezing.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Mimas
data.value: Mimas, a small icy moon of Saturn, with one enormous crater almost a third as wide as the whole moon.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Miranda
data.value: Miranda, a small moon of Uranus with a jumbled-up surface and some of the tallest cliffs in the solar system.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Moon
data.value: The Moon, Earth's only natural satellite. It always shows us the same face, and it's the only other world where people have walked.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Neptune
data.value: Neptune, the farthest planet, with the fastest winds in the solar system. It was found by mathematics before anyone had seen it.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Oberon
data.value: Oberon, the outermost of Uranus's big moons, old and heavily cratered.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Phobos
data.value: Phobos, the bigger of Mars's two little moons. It's slowly spiralling in towards Mars, and one day it will break apart.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Rhea
data.value: Rhea, Saturn's second-biggest moon, a cold, cratered ball of ice and rock.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Saturn
data.value: Saturn, famous for its rings, made of countless chunks of ice and rock. It's so light for its size that it would float in water.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Sun
data.value: The Sun, the star at the centre of our solar system. About a million Earths could fit inside it, and its light takes about eight minutes to reach us.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Tethys
data.value: Tethys, a moon of Saturn made almost entirely of water ice, with a huge canyon stretching most of the way around it.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Titan
data.value: Titan, Saturn's biggest moon. It has a thick orange atmosphere, and lakes and seas of liquid methane.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Titania
data.value: Titania, the biggest moon of Uranus, with great canyons cut across its icy surface.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Triton
data.value: Triton, Neptune's big moon. It goes round the wrong way, which suggests Neptune captured it, and it has geysers that shoot out nitrogen.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Umbriel
data.value: Umbriel, the darkest of Uranus's big moons, with a strange bright ring on its surface.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Uranus
data.value: Uranus, an ice giant tipped right over on its side, so it rolls around the Sun like a ball.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Obj_Venus
data.value: Venus, the hottest planet, even hotter than Mercury. Its thick clouds trap the heat. It also spins backwards, so there the Sun rises in the west.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_01
data.value: This is our solar system, seen from above, with the planets where they really are today. In the middle is the Sun. It holds more than ninety-nine percent of all the mass in the whole solar system.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_02
data.value: The four inner planets, Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, are small and rocky. Earth is the third one out from the Sun.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_03
data.value: Beyond Mars is the asteroid belt: millions of rocky lumps, left over from when the planets formed.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_04
data.value: Then come the giants. Jupiter is the biggest planet by far. More than a thousand Earths would fit inside it.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_05
data.value: Saturn, with its famous rings of ice, is so light for its size that it would float in a big enough bath.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_06
data.value: Far out are the two ice giants, Uranus and Neptune. Neptune takes a hundred and sixty-five years to go once around the Sun.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_07
data.value: In this picture, the planets are spaced out evenly, so they all fit. Think about it: in real life, how far out is Neptune, compared with Earth?

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_08
data.value: About thirty times as far. Now the distances are true to scale. The inner planets huddle close to the Sun, and the outer ones are spread far apart. Even so, the planets themselves are still drawn much too big.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_09
data.value: Let's fly to Earth. Going round it is the Moon, the only other world where people have walked.

data.name: Narr_SolarSystem_Tour_10
data.value: Now you try. Click any planet or moon to fly to it and hear about it.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_01
data.value: This is the Hertzsprung-Russell diagram, one of the most important maps in astronomy. Across is a star's surface temperature, hottest on the left. Up is how bright it really is.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_02
data.value: Most stars lie along this band, the main sequence. They're all doing the same thing: fusing hydrogen in their cores. The heavier the star, the hotter and brighter it is, so the higher up it sits.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_03
data.value: Here's our Sun, right in the middle of the main sequence.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_04
data.value: Up and to the right are the giants. They're cool, but so big that they shine brightly. Arcturus and Aldebaran are giants.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_05
data.value: Down and to the left are the white dwarfs. They're very hot, but tiny, so they're faint. Sirius B is one.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_06
data.value: Think about it. After the main sequence, where will our Sun go on this diagram?

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_07
data.value: Up and to the right. Watch the path it follows. As it runs out of hydrogen in its core, it climbs up to the giants. At the very end, it drops all the way down to the white dwarfs.

data.name: Narr_Star_Diagram_08
data.value: Now you try. Change the star's mass on the left page, and see how its path changes.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_01
data.value: Every star starts in a cloud of gas. But how it ends depends almost entirely on one thing: how much mass it has when it's born.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_02
data.value: The smallest stars, red dwarfs, burn so slowly that they'll last for trillions of years. Not one has died yet in the whole history of the universe.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_03
data.value: Stars like the Sun become red giants, puff off a planetary nebula, and end as white dwarfs.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_04
data.value: Think about it. What happens to a star more than eight times heavier than the Sun?

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_05
data.value: It explodes as a supernova. For a few weeks it can shine brighter than a whole galaxy, and the elements made inside it are blown out into space.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_06
data.value: The core left behind is a neutron star: more mass than the Sun, squeezed into a ball the size of a city.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_07
data.value: And the heaviest stars collapse even further, into a black hole, where gravity is so strong that not even light can escape.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_08
data.value: Now you try. Click a row to choose another kind of star, and follow its life.

data.name: Narr_Star_Fates_09
data.value: The iron in your blood and the calcium in your bones were made inside stars that died long before the Sun was born. We are made of star stuff.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_01
data.value: Every star begins in a cold, dark cloud of gas and dust. Gravity pulls the cloud together. It spins faster and faster, and the middle gets hotter and hotter.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_02
data.value: When the centre reaches about ten million degrees, hydrogen starts fusing into helium, and a star is born. Our Sun has been shining like this for four and a half billion years.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_03
data.value: These dashed circles are the orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, drawn on the same scale, so you can see how big the star gets.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_04
data.value: Think about it. When the hydrogen in its core runs out, what will happen to the Sun?

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_05
data.value: It swells into a red giant, more than a hundred times wider than today. It will swallow Mercury and Venus, and perhaps even Earth.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_06
data.value: Later, it gently puffs its outer layers off into space. They glow around the hot core as a planetary nebula, which, despite the name, has nothing to do with planets.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_07
data.value: What's left is a white dwarf, about the size of Earth but as heavy as half the Sun. It slowly cools and fades for billions and billions of years.

data.name: Narr_Star_Life_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag along the strip of stages at the bottom, and travel through the Sun's whole life.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Agb
data.value: A second giant stage, even bigger than the first. Strong winds blow the star's outer layers away into space.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_BlackHole
data.value: A black hole. In the heaviest stars, nothing can stop the core collapsing. Its gravity becomes so strong that not even light can get out.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_BlueDwarf
data.value: A blue dwarf. No star has become one yet: a red dwarf burns so slowly that it won't get here for trillions of years, far longer than the universe has existed.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_ClassMassive
data.value: Massive stars, about eight to twenty times the Sun's mass. They live for only millions of years, and end in a supernova that leaves a neutron star.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_ClassRedDwarf
data.value: Red dwarfs, less than half the Sun's mass. They're the most common stars of all, and they shine for trillions of years.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_ClassSunLike
data.value: Sun-like stars, from about half to eight times the Sun's mass. They become red giants and end as white dwarfs.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_ClassVeryMassive
data.value: The most massive stars, more than about twenty times the Sun's mass. After their supernova, the core collapses into a black hole.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Giants
data.value: Giants: stars that have run out of hydrogen in their cores and swelled up. They're cool, but so big that they shine brightly.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_HeliumBurning
data.value: Helium burning. The core has become hot enough, about a hundred million degrees, to fuse helium into carbon and oxygen, and the star settles down for a while.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownAldebaran
data.value: Aldebaran, the red eye of Taurus the Bull. It's an orange giant, about forty-five times wider than the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownArcturus
data.value: Arcturus, an orange giant. It has used up the hydrogen in its core and swelled to about twenty-five times the Sun's width.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownBarnard
data.value: Barnard's Star, another nearby red dwarf, about six light-years away. It moves across our sky faster than any other star.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownBetelgeuse
data.value: Betelgeuse, Orion's red shoulder. It's a red supergiant so big that, in the Sun's place, it would reach past the orbit of Mars. One day it will explode as a supernova.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownDeneb
data.value: Deneb, in the constellation of the Swan. It's one of the most luminous stars you can see with the naked eye, about two hundred thousand times as bright as the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownPolaris
data.value: Polaris, the North Star. It's a yellow supergiant that slowly pulses, growing a little brighter and dimmer about every four days.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownProcyonB
data.value: Procyon B, another white dwarf, circling the bright star Procyon. Small and faint, it's the leftover core of a star.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownProxima
data.value: Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, a little over four light-years away. It's a small, cool red dwarf, far too faint to see without a telescope.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownRigel
data.value: Rigel, the bright blue-white foot of Orion. It's a blue supergiant, about a hundred thousand times as bright as the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownSiriusA
data.value: Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. It's a hot, white main-sequence star, about twice the Sun's mass and twenty-five times as bright, less than nine light-years away.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownSiriusB
data.value: Sirius B, the faint companion of Sirius: a white dwarf about the size of Earth, yet about as heavy as the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownSpica
data.value: Spica, a very hot blue star. It's really two massive stars, orbiting each other very closely.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownSun
data.value: The Sun, a middle-aged star on the main sequence, about four and a half billion years old, roughly halfway through its life.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_KnownVega
data.value: Vega, a hot, white main-sequence star about forty times as bright as the Sun, one of the brightest stars of summer evenings.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_LateBurning
data.value: The last fuels. Like the layers of an onion, shells of carbon, neon, oxygen and silicon burn around a growing core of iron. The very last stage lasts only about a day.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_MainSequence
data.value: The main sequence, a star's long, steady adult life. In its core, hydrogen fuses into helium, and the energy this gives out holds the star up against its own gravity.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_MainSequenceBand
data.value: The main sequence. Stars spend most of their lives here, fusing hydrogen in their cores. Heavier stars sit higher up: hotter, bigger, and much brighter.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_NeutronStar
data.value: A neutron star: more mass than the Sun, crushed into a ball the size of a city. Many spin several times a second, sweeping beams across space like a lighthouse. Those are pulsars.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Orbits
data.value: The orbits of Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars, on the same scale. As a red giant, the Sun will reach out to about Earth's orbit.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_PlanetaryNebula
data.value: A planetary nebula: the star's outer layers, thrown off and lit up by the hot core left behind. Through old telescopes they looked a little like planets, which is how they got the name.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Protostar
data.value: A protostar: a ball of gas still pulling itself together inside its cloud. It glows from the heat of falling in, before any fusion has started.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_RedGiant
data.value: A red giant. The star has swelled to a hundred times its old size or more, and its surface has cooled to orange-red. It's still very bright, because it's so big.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_RedSupergiant
data.value: A red supergiant, the biggest kind of star. In the Sun's place, it would swallow all the inner planets.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Subgiant
data.value: A subgiant. The hydrogen in the core has run out, so hydrogen now burns in a shell around it, and the star starts to swell.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_SunToday
data.value: The dashed circle is the Sun as it is today, drawn on the same scale, so you can compare sizes.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Supergiant
data.value: A supergiant. A massive star burns through its fuel fast and swells hugely, crossing the diagram from blue to red.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Supergiants
data.value: Supergiants, the brightest stars of all: massive stars near the end of their short lives.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_Supernova
data.value: A supernova. Iron can't be burned to give out energy, so the core suddenly collapses, and the star blows itself apart. For a few weeks it can outshine a whole galaxy.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_WhiteDwarf
data.value: A white dwarf: the bare core of a Sun-like star, about as big as Earth. A teaspoon of it would weigh about as much as an elephant. It shines only with its leftover heat.

data.name: Narr_Star_Obj_WhiteDwarfs
data.value: White dwarfs: hot but tiny, so they're faint. They're the leftover cores of stars like the Sun.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_01
data.value: Here's Earth seen from above the North Pole, with the Moon going round it. The blue layer is the ocean. Its bulges are hugely exaggerated, so you can see them.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_02
data.value: The Moon pulls on everything on Earth, but not equally. The side facing the Moon is pulled a little harder than Earth's centre, and the far side a little less. These arrows show the difference. It's called the tidal force.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_03
data.value: So the water piles up into a bulge on the side facing the Moon. That's a high tide.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_04
data.value: And here's the surprise: there's a second bulge on the far side. The water there is pulled less than Earth itself, so it gets left behind.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_05
data.value: Earth turns once a day underneath these two bulges. Think about it: how many high tides does a place by the sea get each day?

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_06
data.value: Two. As Earth turns, it carries you through both bulges, so you get two high tides and two low tides a day.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_07
data.value: But the Moon moves along its orbit at the same time, so Earth has to turn a little extra to catch up. That's why high tide comes about fifty minutes later each day.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Bulges_08
data.value: Now you try. Drag sideways across the picture to turn Earth, and watch the water rise and fall where you are.

data.name: Narr_Tides_Coast_01
